https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2el.text: Figure caption, Watch: "Smells really bad" - Residents endure rotting food stench after warehouse fire By Sareen Habeshian Reporting from Los Angeles Published 6 hours ago On any typical day, Alexis Sicairos and his girlfriend have a line of patrons waiting to order a banana buzz latte or a cloud matcha at their Los Angeles coffee stand. But now, the street corner where they sit is largely empty. The reason is clear the second you walk into the neighbourhood: it stinks. On 17 June, a fire destroyed a large cold-storage warehouse in the area, leaving behind some 85 million lb (39 million kg) of rotting food, including beef, pork, poultry and seafood. Nearly two months later, residents of Boyle Heights say the clean-up has taken a lot longer than expected, and they've grown frustrated with the pungent odour hovering over the area. "It smells really bad, like really bad ... to the point that you want to throw up," says Mesha, a 37-year-old security guard stationed outside a marijuana dispensary. She likens the smell to that of a dead body. Lineage, the company that operated the warehouse, said that as of Monday about 80% of the food waste had been removed. But city officials said this week that the company's response "has fallen short", and that they have issued public health and safety violation notices. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Workers have been trying to clean up the rotting food for months "It's been tough," Sicairos, 30, says. After shutting down his coffee stand for two weeks because of the fire, Brew Sting has reopened - but the demand hasn't been the same. He says flies have been swarming relentlessly over the past weeks, since the food that was stored in the warehouse began rotting. The warehouse workers that would previously line up to buy coffee haven't been showing up over the past two months. "Due to the fire, obviously most of them aren't here," Sicairos says. "So we lost those customers, but we also lost customers that don't want to be around the smell, the smoke, the flies. It's understandable. But we have to keep paying our bills, so we're still here." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Rotting food at the warehouse has attracted rats and flies One cannot walk through the area, which is mostly a warehouse district surrounded by homes, without swatting away countless flies, both big and small, including black, blue and green ones. As Sicairos packs up his coffee stand for the day, flies are landing on his tables and his body. He acknowledges that patrons don't want to see flies when they're purchasing food or drinks to consume. A city-commissioned inspection report found that waste and high temperatures at the warehouse could speed up the breeding of flies capable of infecting wounds in both people and animals, a local NBC affiliate reported , external . The report from a pest control company said it could put people and animals with open wounds at risk of contracting disease. People in the community have also reported seeing large rats, and they say traps placed along sidewalks aren't big enough to hold them. Many residents blame the city for what they deem an inadequate response to the fire and a lack of transparency and resources. "I understand why residents are frustrated," Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass told the BBC in a statement. "They deserve transparency, clear communication, and meaningful support. Since day one, I have been in Boyle Heights listening to residents, meeting with families, and making sure their voices guide our response." The mayor, who is up for re-election this year, said she directed city departments to work with local, state, federal, nonprofit and community partners to deliver immediate support and solutions. Bass has also issued executive orders to mobilise resources and speed up the cleaning process. The city says they and other local partners have brought mobile health clinics to the neighbourhood and delivered thousands of air purifiers. Late last month, the county's public health department fined Lineage for "unsanitary and nuisance" conditions with $500-a-day citations. The mayor has given Lineage a 13 August deadline to complete the cleanup. The company said on Monday they are 80% of the way there - up from 60% on July 31. "Our goal is to complete bulk food waste removal from the site next week," a Lineage spokesperson told the BBC on Wednesday. They expect to spend between $80 million to $100 million on the cleanup. Outside the warehouse, dozens of workers in hard hats and neon vests can be seen tackling the effort, some wearing face coverings. Officials with the local air quality authority and sheriff's office were also on site. Image source, Getty Images In an letter shared on Tuesday, Bass said the company's response "has fallen short". "Residents, public agencies, and elected officials have repeatedly sought timely information regarding the cleanup, remediation, environmental monitoring, and recovery," Bass wrote in the letter to Lineage shareholders. "Too often, those requests have been met with delayed communication, limited transparency, and insufficient public engagement". The mayor also directed city departments to halt plans to rebuild the warehouse "until the health and safety of the community are protected". Lineage, which is a temperature-controlled warehousing and logistics company, says "cleanup crews are working around the clock to remove food waste, clear debris and dismantle damaged sections of the structure. "However, this is a highly complex operation," they say, adding that reducing odours is a "key priority" in their cleanup effort. Beállítom Videóban vette védelmébe az alakuló Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatalt a miniszterelnök, mivel fontosnak tartotta, hogy elmondja a véleményét „az utóbbi napok eseményei, hírei és álhírei” miatt. Az elsíbolt vagyonok visszaszerzését, valamint a felelősök megbüntetését a Tisza egyik legfőbb vállalásának nevezte. Az Országgyűlés mai döntését a megválasztott elnök és nyomozati elnökhelyettes kapcsán természetesen lehet vitatni, lehet kritizálni – mondta Magyar – de azt állítani, hogy a mai döntés miatt veszélybe került volna a rendszerváltás egyik legfőbb feladata és vállalása, „egyszerűen helytelen”. Magyar szerint a vezetést a jövőben tettei és eredményei alapján kell megítélni. A miniszterelnök meggyőződése, hogy a kiválasztási folyamat szakmai és transzparens volt: „Az imént beszéltem telefonon Ligeti Miklóssal, aki megerősítette számomra, hogy ő is alkotmányosnak, törvényesnek és fairnek tartotta az eljárást”. Megemlítette, hogy a maffia ellen küzdeni, nyomozni az egyik legveszélyesebb dolog ezért kapnak a hivatal vezetői 24 órás személyi védelmet a rendőrségtől. Magyar többeknek is üzent. Egyrészt azoknak a közéleti szereplőknek – volt országgyűlési képviselőknek, korábbi kormánytagoknak – akik az elmúlt napokban megpróbálták hitelteleníteni a hivatalt és annak vezetőjét. „Azt üzenem, hogy gondolják meg, hogy mit tesznek” – mondta a miniszterelnök. „Aki már a rajtvonalnál megpróbálja elgáncsolni azokat, akiknek a közvagyon visszaszerzése lesz a dolguk, annak később nehéz lesz megmagyaráznia, hogy valójában kinek az érdekét is szolgálta” – fogalmazott. És üzent a Tisza közösségének is, méghozzá azt, hogy ugyan lehet az Országgyűlés mai döntését kritizálni, de „megkérdőjelezni a képviselők vagy akár a kormánytagok rendszerváltás iránti elkötelezettségét és a munkáját rendkívül igazságtalan és méltánytalan”. A miniszterelnök eredményes munkát kívánt az új és leendő dolgozóknak. „Dolgozzanak bátran, dolgozzanak szabadon, dolgozzanak úgy, hogy néhány év múlva egyetlen magyar embernek se kelljen azt mondania többé, amit az elmúlt évtizedekben annyiszor hallottunk, hogy ebben az országban úgysem történik semmi: mert most történni fog” – zárta a videót Magyar Péter. Photograph: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A fire burns at a Wildberries' logistics complex, outside Moscow. Zelenskyy has ordered his military to launch 1,000 long-range strikes on Russia every day. Photograph: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy orders military to triple daily long-range strikes on Russia Kyiv to ramp up attacks; Russian gasoline production drops after drone strikes; Fedorov joins Italy’s defence ministry. What we know on day 1,648 Guardian staff and agencies Fri 28 Aug 2026 21.26 EDT Last modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 21.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google ⁠Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ⁠​he has ⁠ordered his military to increase its ⁠long-range ​drone ‌strikes ‌against Russia to ‌1,000 per day , up from about 300 currently. “There ‌needs to be more: ​there is a concrete goal, ⁠and we will fulfil ​this ​task,” the Ukrainian president ​declared ​on Friday in ‌his ​evening address. Russia’s ⁠gasoline production fell ​to about 70% of domestic consumption levels by the end of August after a series of drone attacks forced major refineries to suspend operations, according to two ⁠industry sources who spoke to Reuters. After a brief respite at the end of July, when some local authorities ​began easing or lifting restrictions on fuel sales, shortages ‌returned to Russian regions in ‌August. Over the past week, drones ‌struck and halted operations at several major refineries, including plants in Perm, Nizhny Novgorod and Yaroslavl, all significant producers of motor gasoline. Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit , western officials have said. While Russia is still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the past two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured, Peter Walker writes . Recent Russian air attacks have destroyed about 90% of retailers’ food logistics in Ukraine , ⁠Kyiv’s agricultural minister said on Friday. Both countries have stepped up strikes in recent weeks on economic targets such as major retailers, with Russia targeting warehouses for ⁠Ukraine’s premier supermarket chains, ⁠top postal service and home-goods ​stores. “As of today, roughly speaking, 90% of food logistics operated by retail chains have been destroyed, but that doesn’t mean Ukrainians will be left without food,” farm minister Taras Vysotskyi was cited by ⁠the Ukrinform agency as saying. His comments to reporters in Kyiv are the most frank official assessment of the damage Russia’s escalating strikes have brought on Ukraine’s increasingly fragile economy in the fifth year of war. Ukraine has stored ⁠14.6bn cubic metres ​of gas ⁠in underground storage, enough ⁠for ​the upcoming ‌winter ‌season , the ‌country’s energy minister said. “Ukraine has stockpiled ‌natural gas for ​the baseline scenario for getting ⁠through the ​winter,” Denys ​Shmyhal ​said ​on Friday. Authorities ⁠in Russia’s Rostov region ⁠declared a ⁠state ​of emergency on Friday , ⁠saying port closures and disruptions ⁠to navigation ​in ‌the ‌Azov-Black Sea basin had ‌led to a significant accumulation of agricultural products at farms. The ‌regional government said on ​Telegram an emergency response had been introduced ⁠across the ​region, without ​going into ​more detail. Ukraine’s former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has ⁠accepted a role as innovation adviser at Italy’s Defence Ministry , officials said ⁠on ​Friday. Italy’s defence minister Guido Crosetto had disclosed the offer shortly after Fedorov ⁠was dismissed in July. Fedorov, 35, was fired six months after his appointment, having ​initiated reforms around procurement and mobilisation that put him on a collision course with the military establishment and political rivals. The UN nuclear ⁠watchdog said on Friday it had ⁠been informed ⁠of ​three drone incidents at Russian-held Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear power plant in south-eastern Ukraine ⁠earlier this week. The International ​Atomic ‌Energy Agency said a drone attack ‌on 25 August reportedly occurred near the plant’s cooling pond, injuring two plant employees, ‌while two other drones on 26 August ​reportedly struck the site’s dry spent nuclear fuel storage area ⁠and the sprinkling ​device of ​the power ​units system. Radiation levels at ​the ‌Zaporizhzhia ​plant ​remained normal, the watchdog added. Russian forces on Friday resumed their drone barrage of Ukraine’s Kyiv region, hitting more than a dozen apartment buildings and storage depots in a second straight day of aerial attacks , officials said. Russian strikes in the Kyiv region damaged 14 warehouses, 16 private houses, three apartment buildings and 16 vehicles, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv regional military administration, said Friday. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: A car burns at Place de la République during a protest on 17 October 2026. Photograph: Thibault Camus/AP View image in fullscreen A car burns at Place de la République during a protest on 17 October 2026. Photograph: Thibault Camus/AP Opinion France The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment Editorial The scenes of social unrest and violence at the weekend are an ominous portent, ahead of elections which may deliver a far-right presidency Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.30 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.35 EDT Share I n Emmanuel Macron’s book Revolution , published ahead of the 2017 presidential election that he went on to win, he promised to restore hope to a country that was losing faith in its future. As Mr Macron’s lame-duck second term enters its last phase against a quasi-insurrectionary backdrop of torched public buildings and looted shops, the failure of that political project appears total. The worst scenes of urban violence for years overshadowed a weekend of protest that gravely undermined what is left of the French president’s authority. As police lost control of the streets, more than 2,000 shops were ransacked. Far-left groups targeted town halls and local buildings, and engaged in pitched battles with the police, whose disastrously heavy-handed response to last week’s high school protests has succeeded only in escalating tensions. View image in fullscreen Emmanuel Macron. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/AFP/Getty In a statement on Sunday evening, Mr Macron rightly condemned what he described as episodes of “unbridled violence”. On the far right, Marine Le Pen is already exploiting a national sense of dismay to present herself as the law-and-order solution to the crisis. But the shocking actions of a minority should not obscure the significance of the vast, peaceful demonstrations that took place throughout France on Saturday. Calls to unite the student protests and the yellow vest movement, which disrupted Mr Macron’s first term over cost of living issues, mobilised up to 800,000 people. The root cause of the unrest is a widespread perception that France’s social contract is broken. The young feel let down by an underfunded and unequal education system, and are fearful of the future impact of AI and the climate emergency. As is increasingly the case across Europe, they no longer trust mainstream politicians to find answers. The scale of the weekend protests showed that gen Z’s discontent has merged with that felt in the country’s neglected towns and banlieues , which have suffered repeated economic shocks since the Covid pandemic. The obtuse and stubborn response from Mr Macron has been to double down on a cost‑cutting agenda to reduce France’s public debt, in order to appease the financial markets. But in an era where the asset-rich have continued to flourish, and the wealthiest have done best of all, to argue that that there is no alternative to spending less on schools and healthcare won’t wash. The economist Thomas Piketty pointed out during last week’s student protests that the boom in private wealth means that, despite the size of its public debt, “France has never been richer”. Mr Macron’s reckless decision to call a snap election in 2024, which cost him his majority, left him a diminished political figure. His biggest subsequent error has been to haughtily persist with the economics of austerity, despite clear evidence of deepening political polarisation and rising popular anger. With each week that passes, the social consequences appear more ominous, ahead of presidential elections in six months’ time. The latest polls suggest that the far right’s huge lead is widening ahead of that contest. Meanwhile, the hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon continues to outscore progressive rivals, though the numbers suggest that he would heavily lose a runoff against Ms Le Pen. In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.
